INSIDE Earth.

A descent through the planet under your feet. Scroll down and don't look back.

Begin descent
Chapter 1 0 km

The calm lie of the surface What you see is hiding what you are standing on.

Earth looks calm from the surface. Most days the ground feels solid. Roads stay where they are. Mountains do not seem to move. The floor does not ripple like water.

That calm is misleading.

Deep under your feet, Earth is hot, layered, pressurized, and slowly moving. Continents drift. Ocean floors spread. Mountains rise. Earthquakes snap through rock. Liquid metal churns thousands of kilometers below us and helps build the invisible shield that surrounds the whole planet.

Earth is not just a rock floating in space. It is an active planet.

Scientists describe Earth's inside two ways at the same time. One way asks: what is each layer made of? That gives us three big chemical layers, the crust, the mantle, and the core. The other way asks: how does each layer behave? That gives us the lithosphere, the asthenosphere, the deeper mantle, the outer core, and the inner core.

That sounds simple. Wait until you see what is actually going on.

Pause & Picture

Stand still for a second. Imagine you could see straight down through the floor, through the dirt, through everything, all the way to the center of the planet. You would be looking through more than 6,000 kilometers of stuff. How much of it do you think is solid? How much is liquid? Make a guess before you keep scrolling.

Chapter 2 how we know

Scanning the planet with earthquakes Nobody has ever been there.

Here is a slightly strange fact. Nobody has visited Earth's core. Nobody has drilled even close to where the mantle meets the core. The deepest drill holes ever made barely scratch the crust compared with the whole planet's diameter.

So how do scientists actually know what is inside Earth?

They use earthquakes.

When an earthquake happens, it sends energy in every direction. These bursts of energy are called seismic waves, and they move through the planet like ripples through a giant body, except the body is made of rock and metal.

Different materials change the speed, direction, and behavior of those waves. By recording earthquakes from all over the world and comparing what arrived where, scientists basically gave Earth an ultrasound.

WaveWhat it doesWhy it matters
P-wavesPush and pull material, like squeezing and stretching a slinkyThey travel through solids and liquids
S-wavesShake material side to sideThey travel through solids but not through liquids

That second fact does a lot of heavy lifting. Because S-waves cannot pass through liquid, scientists noticed they kept vanishing in a certain ring-shaped zone after every big earthquake. The only thing that explained it was a giant region of liquid sitting deep inside the planet.

That is how we discovered the outer core. Not by drilling. By listening.

Earthquakes are not just disasters. They are also accidental planet scanners.

Quick Check

If S-waves can travel through solids but not liquids, what does the fact that S-waves disappear after passing through one part of Earth tell us about that part?

It tells us that part of Earth is liquid, since S-waves cannot make it through. That's how scientists figured out that the outer core is liquid metal, without ever going there.
Chapter 3 0 to 70 km

The skin of the apple You live on something thinner than you think.

The crust is Earth's outermost rocky layer. Continents, ocean floors, mountains, valleys, plains, deserts, the ground under your house, all of it is crust.

The crust is thin. Embarrassingly thin.

Compared with the whole planet, the crust is more like the skin on an apple than the apple itself. Under the oceans, it is often only about 5 kilometers thick. Under the continents, it is much thicker but still nothing compared with what is below it.

TypeWherePersonality
Oceanic crustUnder the oceansThinner, denser, mostly basalt, usually younger
Continental crustUnder the continentsThicker, less dense, more granite-like, often very old

One thing that trips a lot of people up: the crust is not the same thing as a tectonic plate. A tectonic plate includes the crust plus the cold, rigid top of the mantle below it. That whole stiff package is the lithosphere, and we'll get there in a few chapters.

Memory hook Crust = a chemical label (what it's made of). Lithosphere = a mechanical label (how it behaves). They overlap, but they are not the same thing. Hold onto that. You'll see why soon.
Chapter 4 ~70 to 2,900 km

The engine room The mantle is not what you think it is.

The mantle sits below the crust and above the core. By volume, it is by far the largest part of Earth, around 84 percent of the planet's volume. The crust, for comparison, is about 1 percent.

If you grew up picturing the mantle as a giant underground ocean of lava, you have plenty of company. Movies, cartoons, even some textbooks have sold that idea for decades.

It's wrong.

The mantle is mostly solid rock. Hot, deep, pressurized solid rock. But it's a kind of solid that, over very long timescales, can slowly bend and flow.

Think of something tough and stiff but not quite frozen, something that, given enough heat, pressure, and millions of years, can squish and creep. The mantle does not slosh around like water. It moves much more slowly than that. But it does move, and that movement is the reason the surface of Earth is not still.

The mantle is made mostly of silicate minerals, rocks rich in silicon, oxygen, magnesium, and iron. As you go deeper, the temperature climbs and the pressure climbs much faster. Rock near the top of the mantle does not behave like rock far down at the bottom of the mantle. We will keep coming back to this idea.

Pause & Wonder

Solid rock that flows. Slowly. Without melting. Over millions of years. Does that even count as solid? Where exactly is the line between "solid" and "liquid" when you change the timescale enough?

Quick Check

What's wrong with the picture of the mantle as a giant ocean of lava?

The mantle is mostly solid rock, not liquid. It is extremely hot and under huge pressure, so over very long timescales it can slowly deform, but it doesn't slosh around like water. Tiny amounts of melt can form in special places, but the mantle is not a lava ocean.
Chapter 5 ~2,900 to 6,378 km

Crushed by pressure The most counterintuitive layer in the whole planet.

At Earth's center is the core. It is mostly iron and nickel, an enormous ball of metal sitting at the heart of the planet. And it is not one thing. It is two.

LayerStateMain materialWhy it matters
Outer coreLiquidIron and nickelGenerates Earth's magnetic field
Inner coreSolidIron and nickelSolid only because the pressure is enormous

The outer core is liquid because it is brutally hot, hot enough that the iron and nickel there are melted.

The inner core is also brutally hot. Hotter, even. By every rule of thumb you have ever met, it ought to be liquid too. But it isn't. It is solid.

The inner core is solid not because it is cold. It is solid because it is crushed.

At Earth's center, the pressure is so unbelievably high that it forces the metal atoms to pack themselves into a rigid, locked structure. Heat says melt. Pressure says no, you don't. At the very center of the planet, pressure wins.

Pause & Wonder

Heat usually wins. Heat melts ice cream, melts metal, melts almost anything if it's hot enough. But at Earth's center, something is hotter than anything in your everyday life and still solid, because so much weight is sitting on top of it. What other places in the universe might that happen?

Quick Check

Two of your friends are arguing. One says the inner core is solid because it's the coldest part of Earth. The other says it's solid because of pressure. Who is right, and why?

The pressure friend is right. The inner core is extremely hot, hotter than the surface of the Sun in some estimates. But it is also under such enormous pressure that the atoms get packed too tightly to move freely as a liquid. So it ends up solid, despite being scorching hot.
Chapter 6 two maps

Two ways to slice the same planet Chemistry asks what. Mechanics asks how.

This is one of the most important ideas in this whole lesson. So slow down.

Scientists do not have just one way to label Earth's insides. They have two. Each one answers a different question.

Layer systemThe question it answersExamples
ChemicalWhat is this layer made of?Crust, mantle, core
MechanicalHow does this layer behave?Lithosphere, asthenosphere, outer core, inner core

That distinction is why we can say things like: the lithosphere includes the crust and part of the upper mantle. Same general region, two different questions, two different answers.

Mantle rock near the very top is cool enough to be rigid. So even though it is chemically part of the mantle, mechanically it is part of the same stiff slab as the crust. Together they make the lithosphere. Below that, the same kind of rock is hotter and can slowly flow. That is the asthenosphere.

Same rock, different rulebook.

Quick Check

Why isn't the lithosphere just another word for the crust?

Because the lithosphere is a behavior label, not a chemistry label. It includes the crust and the cool, stiff top of the mantle. The crust by itself is only a chemical label. They overlap, but the lithosphere goes a little deeper.
Chapter 7 0 to ~100 km

Earth's broken shell You are walking on a giant cracked egg.

The lithosphere is Earth's rigid outer shell. It is the crust plus the top, stiff part of the mantle.

And it is broken.

Not damaged broken. By design broken. The lithosphere is split into enormous pieces called tectonic plates. There are roughly a dozen big ones and a bunch of smaller ones, and they all slide around very slowly over the weaker layer beneath them.

These plates do not float on lava. They are big slabs of rock riding on top of more rock, just rock that happens to be hot enough to slowly flow. We are about to meet that lower layer in a second.

Plates move slowly. Usually only a few centimeters per year. That sounds like nothing. But Earth has been doing this for billions of years, and a few centimeters per year, given enough time, will:

  • ↳ open oceans
  • ↳ close oceans
  • ↳ raise mountains
  • ↳ destroy mountains
  • ↳ split continents
  • ↳ smash continents together
  • ↳ trigger earthquakes
  • ↳ feed volcanoes

The lithosphere is Earth's cracked armor. The cracks are where the action lives.

Pause & Picture

Your fingernails grow about as fast as tectonic plates move. So next time you trim them, imagine that in the same amount of time those nails grew, an entire continent has shifted that same distance. The whole world. By that much. That much is enough.

Chapter 8 ~100 to ~410 km

The layer that lets it all move Without this, nothing on the surface changes.

Beneath the lithosphere is the asthenosphere. It is part of the upper mantle. It is not liquid, but it is hotter, weaker, and able to slowly flow.

A simple way to keep them straight:

  • Lithosphere = rigid. Breakable. Can crack and snap.
  • Asthenosphere = solid, but bendable. Can slowly squish and reshape.

The asthenosphere is what lets the tectonic plates move at all. Without that softer, deformable layer underneath, the rigid plates would have nothing to slide around on. Plate tectonics literally could not happen.

Misconception alert Tectonic plates are not surfing on lava. The asthenosphere is mostly solid rock. It is just hot enough, and under just the right pressure, to slowly creep. Think of it less like an ocean and more like very, very stiff caramel.
Chapter 9 where the action happens

The surface is moving And it has been the entire time.

Plate tectonics is the idea that Earth's lithosphere is broken into moving plates. Most of the dramatic things that happen on Earth's surface, the earthquakes, the volcanoes, the mountain ranges, the ocean trenches, happen along the edges of these plates. Those edges are called plate boundaries, and there are three main flavors.

Plates can move apart. They can move together. Or they can slide past each other. Each kind of boundary does something very different. Let's take them one at a time.

Chapter 10 divergent boundaries

When plates pull apart This is where new Earth gets made.

At a divergent boundary, two plates move away from each other. Hot rock from below rises into the gap, cools off, and becomes brand new crust.

Most of this happens at the bottom of the ocean. The Atlantic Ocean is currently getting wider by a few centimeters every year because of a divergent boundary running right down its middle: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

At a divergent boundary, you will usually find new crust forming, some volcanic activity, shallow earthquakes, ocean ridges, and in places where it happens on land instead of under the sea, valleys called rifts.

Earth is constantly building new crust. You just can't see it, because most of it happens 3,000 meters underwater.

Chapter 11 convergent boundaries

When plates collide Something always has to give.

At a convergent boundary, two plates push toward each other. What happens next depends on which two plates are involved.

Who's collidingWhat usually happens
Oceanic plate vs. continental plateThe denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the continent.
Oceanic plate vs. oceanic plateOne ocean plate sinks beneath the other. Volcanic island arcs can form.
Continental plate vs. continental plateNeither side sinks easily. Both crumple upward. Mountains rise.

When one plate sinks beneath another, that process has a name: subduction. Subduction is one of Earth's recycling systems. The descending plate gets dragged back down into the mantle, where it is heated, transformed, and over time its material gets reused.

When two continental plates collide instead, neither one is dense enough to sink, so both crumple upward like two cars in a head-on crash. That is how the Himalayas formed. India crashed into Asia, very slowly, and the rock had nowhere to go but up.

At convergent boundaries you will find deep ocean trenches, powerful earthquakes, volcanic arcs, mountain ranges, and subduction zones, all the most dramatic features of the planet, basically.

Earth doesn't just create rock. It also recycles it.

Quick Check

Why do the Himalayas keep growing, instead of one plate just sliding under the other and finishing the job?

Because both colliding plates are continental, and continental crust is too thick and too low in density for either plate to sink easily into the mantle. So instead, the rock crumples upward. India is still pushing into Asia today, which is why the Himalayas are still rising.
Chapter 12 transform boundaries

When plates grind past Nothing built. Nothing destroyed. Just stress.

At a transform boundary, two plates slide sideways past each other. They don't pull apart. They don't slam together. They grind.

The most famous example is the San Andreas Fault in California, where the Pacific Plate is sliding past the North American Plate.

Plates at a transform boundary don't slide smoothly. They jam against each other. Stress builds up. And builds. And builds. Then suddenly, with no warning, they slip. That sudden release of stored stress is an earthquake.

Transform boundaries are not usually known for volcanoes (no plate is sinking, so nothing is melting), but they are some of the most active earthquake zones on Earth.

Three boundaries, three personalities Divergent: builders. They make new crust.
Convergent: destroyers and crumplers. They recycle crust and pile up mountains.
Transform: grinders. They store stress and release it in earthquakes.
Chapter 13 the engine, revealed

Why anything moves at all What's actually pushing the plates around?

There isn't one single force moving the plates. Several connected things in Earth's interior all push and pull at once.

ForceWhat it actually means
Mantle convectionHot mantle rock rises. Cooler rock sinks. The whole thing slowly circulates in cells.
Slab pullA cold, heavy plate sinking at a subduction zone drags the rest of the plate behind it.
Ridge pushNewly made crust at a mid-ocean ridge slides downhill away from the high ridge.
Gravity & densityDenser stuff sinks. Lighter stuff rises. Always. Everywhere.

Tectonic plates move at different speeds, generally somewhere between 2 and 15 centimeters per year. That sounds tiny. It is tiny, by the standards of a human life. But Earth doesn't run on a human schedule.

Slow does not mean small. It just means patient.

Chapter 14 the invisible shield

The shield you can't see But it's the reason your compass works.

Earth has a magnetic field. You can't see it directly, but it's everywhere around you and stretches out into space for tens of thousands of kilometers.

You've already used it. Every compass on the planet works because a small magnet lines itself up with Earth's magnetosphere. That's why a compass needle reliably points (mostly) north.

Magnetic north is not in exactly the same place as the geographic North Pole. And it isn't even sitting still. Magnetic north moves a little bit every year. Over very long timescales, Earth's magnetic field has even flipped completely, multiple times. North became south. South became north. We're not making that up.

The field moves because the thing creating it moves. And what's creating it is something we've already met, way down in the outer core.

Chapter 15 ~5,000 km

The hidden generator Inside the outer core, an electrical engine is running.

The process that creates Earth's magnetic field has a name: the geodynamo. And it is one of the strangest, coolest machines in the solar system, because nobody built it. It runs by itself.

Here is the chain of logic, six steps, in order:

  1. Earth's outer core is liquid metal.
  2. That liquid metal is mostly iron and nickel.
  3. It moves because of heat (rising hot stuff, sinking cooler stuff) and Earth's rotation.
  4. Moving electrically conductive fluid can generate electric currents.
  5. Electric currents generate magnetic fields. Always. It's a basic law of physics.
  6. Result: a giant, planet-sized magnet, made of nothing but moving metal.

This isn't magic. It's physics. Moving conductors create magnetic fields. We use the same principle to build electric generators on the surface. Earth just happens to have a generator the size of the Moon, running 24 hours a day, with no human attending it. It has been running for billions of years.

A magnet made of nothing but moving metal.

Pause & Wonder

If you wanted to break Earth's magnetic field, what would you have to do? Where in the chain above is the weakest link? Could a planet ever lose its magnetic field for real?

Chapter 16 why you should care

Why the magnetic field matters It's not just for compasses.

The magnetic field is not a force field from a sci-fi movie. It does not make Earth invincible. It does not block every threat from space. (The atmosphere helps a lot too.)

But the magnetic field does deflect the steady stream of charged particles flying out from the Sun, called the solar wind. Without that deflection, the upper atmosphere of Earth would interact with the solar wind very differently. Over time, we might lose more of our atmosphere to space.

And when some of those charged particles do sneak in, near the poles, they hit gas molecules in the upper atmosphere and make them glow. That's an aurora: the northern and southern lights. So every time someone sees the aurora, they're seeing the magnetic field working, live, in real time.

Chapter 17 zoom out

The whole planet, in one breath None of it works alone.

Earth's layers are not separate chapters. They are connected. Pull on one thread, and something else moves.

  • → The core releases heat.
  • → The mantle uses that heat to slowly convect.
  • → The asthenosphere deforms and lets plates ride.
  • → The lithosphere cracks into plates.
  • → The plates collide, split, and slide.
  • → The boundaries make earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountains.
  • → The outer core, churning, makes the magnetic field.
  • → The magnetic field deflects the solar wind.
  • → The solar wind, sneaking in at the poles, makes the auroras.

A change deep inside the planet can change what happens in the sky. Everything is connected.

Chapter 18 myth busters

Six things almost everybody gets wrong If you believed any of these, you have company.

The mantle is liquid lava.

Mostly solid rock. Hot, deep, and slowly deformable, but not a lava ocean. A little melt happens in special spots, but the bulk of the mantle is solid.

The crust and the lithosphere are the same thing.

The crust is a chemistry label. The lithosphere is a behavior label. The lithosphere includes the crust plus the cool, stiff top of the mantle.

The whole core is liquid.

The outer core is liquid. The inner core is solid. Same metal, different states, because of pressure.

The inner core is solid because it's cooler.

The inner core is extremely hot. It's solid because the pressure at the center of Earth is enormous. Pressure beats heat at the core.

Tectonic plates move fast.

Plates move at fingernail-growing speeds, usually centimeters per year. Over millions of years, that's enough to rebuild the map of the world.

Earth's magnetic field never changes.

Magnetic north wanders. The field weakens and strengthens. The whole thing has even completely flipped, many times, throughout Earth's history.

Chapter 19 vocab review

Words that paid for themselves The vocabulary, all in one place.

CrustEarth's thin, solid outer rock layer.
MantleThick layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath the crust.
CoreEarth's central metal-rich region. Outer core liquid, inner core solid.
LithosphereRigid outer layer made of crust + uppermost mantle.
AsthenosphereHot, weak upper mantle layer that can slowly flow.
Outer coreLiquid metal layer beneath the mantle.
Inner coreSolid metal center of Earth.
Plate tectonicsTheory that Earth's lithosphere is broken into moving plates.
Tectonic plateA large piece of Earth's lithosphere.
ConvectionHot stuff rising, cool stuff sinking.
SubductionOne plate sinking beneath another.
Divergent boundaryPlates moving apart.
Convergent boundaryPlates moving together.
Transform boundaryPlates sliding past each other.
GeodynamoThe process that creates Earth's magnetic field.
MagnetosphereRegion around Earth controlled by its magnetic field.
Seismic wavesEarthquake waves used to study Earth's interior.

Part 5 · Essay

Explain how Earth's inner layers connect to what happens on the surface and around the planet. Use as many of these terms as you can: crust, mantle, lithosphere, asthenosphere, outer core, inner core, convection, plate tectonics, geodynamo.

A strong answer would mention that heat inside Earth drives convection in the mantle; that tectonic plates ride over the asthenosphere; that plate boundaries are where earthquakes, volcanoes, mountains, and trenches form; and that moving liquid metal in the outer core generates Earth's magnetic field through the geodynamo.
